f-date.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-panic.claim: When news reached the Greek fleet at Salamis that the Acropolis had fallen, some commanders panicked and voted to sail away to the Isthmus.

f-sicinnus-who.claim: Sicinnus was a slave of Themistocles' household and the tutor of his children.

f-sicinnus-message.claim: Themistocles sent him by boat to the Persian commanders with a message: Themistocles was on the king's side, and the Greeks were terrified and planning to flee.

f-sicinnus-bait.claim: The message said that if the Persians stopped the Greeks escaping, they would see them fighting among themselves.

f-aeschylus-message.claim: Aeschylus, eight years later, also tells of a Greek who came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would slip away under cover of night.

f-night-move.claim: The Persians believed it: that night they moved their ships to close the channels around Salamis and landed soldiers on the islet of Psyttaleia.

f-aristides.claim: Aristides, Themistocles' old rival who had been ostracised from Athens, crossed from Aegina and brought word that the fleet was surrounded.

f-sicinnus-reward.claim: Afterwards Themistocles made Sicinnus a citizen of Thespiae and a rich man.

f-trap.claim: Modern historians read the message as a deliberate trap to force the battle into the narrow strait.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-narrows.claim: In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.

f-trap-why.claim: Themistocles sent the message when he was losing the council debate to the Peloponnesian commanders, who wanted to leave Salamis and fight at the Isthmus.
